pos: proper n. (Hebrew name of Hosea’s daughter, a sign-name)
etymology: Hebrew lo' ruchamah, from lo', not, and racham, to have compassion, to show tender mercy: not pitied, she that hath not obtained mercy.
biblical_def: The second child of Hosea and Gomer bore a sentence for a name. “And she conceived again, and bare a daughter. And God said unto him, Call her name Loruhamah: for I will no more have mercy upon the house of Israel; but I will utterly take them away” (Hosea 1:6). Every time the girl was called in from the field, the northern kingdom heard its verdict. Yet the same prophet who named her carried the reversal in his scroll: “and I will have mercy upon her that had not obtained mercy; and I will say to them which were not my people, Thou art my people” (Hosea 2:23). Peter takes that promise and lays it on scattered believers, Jew and Gentile alike: “which had not obtained mercy, but now have obtained mercy” (1 Peter 2:10). Loruhamah is therefore the name of every sinner before grace, and the gospel is God renaming her.

webster_full: Webster (1828) gives no entry for Loruhamah.

corruption_summary: Hosea's sign-names are read as belonging to national Israel alone, sealed off from the church, when Peter and Paul expressly apply them to the believing Gentiles.
corruption_paragraphs: The dispensational scheme of Darby and Scofield keeps Israel and the church on two separate tracks, so that Hosea's promises of renewed mercy must wait for a future national restoration and cannot rightly belong to Gentile believers now. The apostles read the prophet otherwise. Peter writes to the elect strangers of the dispersion that they have obtained mercy, and Paul cites Hosea in Romans 9:25 to explain why God has called vessels of mercy not of the Jews only, but also of the Gentiles.

The dictionary follows the apostolic hermeneutic. One people of God is gathered in Christ from both Israel and the nations, and the reversal of Loruhamah is fulfilled wherever the gospel calls the unpitied into mercy. To push it wholly into a future millennial program is to read Hosea against the very apostles who interpreted him.

pos: proper n. (Hebrew name of Hosea’s second son, a sign-name)
etymology: Hebrew lo' 'ammi, from lo', not, and 'am, people, with the first-person suffix: not my people.
biblical_def: Hosea's third child carried the hardest name of the three. “Then said God, Call his name Loammi: for ye are not my people, and I will not be your God” (Hosea 1:9). The covenant formula, I will be your God and ye shall be my people, is turned inside out and stamped on a baby. Israel had gone after Baalim, and the LORD declared the marriage broken in the name of a child. Yet the very next verse refuses to let the sentence stand as the last word: “in the place where it was said unto them, Ye are not my people, there it shall be said unto them, Ye are the sons of the living God” (Hosea 1:10). Paul quotes the promise to explain how Gentiles enter: “I will call them my people, which were not my people” (Romans 9:25). Loammi is the plain truth about man outside the covenant, and adoption is God's answer to it.

webster_full: Webster (1828) gives no entry for Loammi.

Rom 9:25

corruption_summary: The name is softened into a temporary misunderstanding, when it was a judicial sentence that only sovereign grace could reverse.
corruption_paragraphs: Modern preaching, embarrassed by divine wrath, likes to treat Loammi as if God were only voicing Israel's feelings about herself. The text will not allow it. God Himself gives the name, God Himself gives the reason, and the reason is the breach of covenant by an idolatrous people.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition beyond that softening. The principle to recover is adoption: those who were not a people are made sons of the living God by grace alone, not by any recovery of their own. Loammi is overturned only by the God who pronounced it.

pos: proper n. (Hebrew sign-name of Isaiah’s son)
etymology: Hebrew maher shalal chash baz: maher, hasten; shalal, spoil; chash, hurry; baz, prey. Roughly, swift is the spoil, speedy the prey. The longest personal name in the Bible.
biblical_def: Before the child was born his name was written large in public. “Moreover the LORD said unto me, Take thee a great roll, and write in it with a man's pen concerning Mahershalalhashbaz” (Isaiah 8:1). Witnesses were taken, and then: “And I went unto the prophetess; and she conceived, and bare a son. Then said the LORD to me, Call his name Mahershalalhashbaz” (Isaiah 8:3). The name was a dated prophecy against the alliance of Syria and Ephraim that frightened Ahaz: “For before the child shall have knowledge to cry, My father, and my mother, the riches of Damascus and the spoil of Samaria shall be taken away before the king of Assyria” (Isaiah 8:4). Damascus fell to Assyria in 732 BC, and Samaria within the decade. The prophet and his children stood in Israel as signs (Isaiah 8:18), and this boy's name was a clock the LORD set running in public view.

webster_full: Webster (1828) gives no entry for Mahershalalhashbaz.

corruption_summary: Critics fold this child into Isaiah 7:14 and make him the whole fulfillment of the Immanuel sign, emptying the virgin birth of its prophecy.
corruption_paragraphs: A common move in modern commentary is to say that the son born to the prophetess in Isaiah 8 simply is the child of Isaiah 7:14, so that the Immanuel prophecy was exhausted in the eighth century and Matthew merely borrowed it. That reading collapses two distinct signs. The child of Isaiah 7 is born of a virgin and bears the name God with us; the child of Isaiah 8 is born to the prophet's wife and bears a name of plunder.

Matthew 1:23 is not an apostolic misreading but the inspired interpretation: the virgin conceived and bare a son, and His name is Immanuel. Mahershalalhashbaz was a true near sign that Ahaz's enemies would fall on schedule, which is exactly why the far sign of the virgin's Son could be trusted.

pos: proper n. (Hebrew name: of a queen of Judah, and a prophetic name of Zion)
etymology: Hebrew chephtsi-bah, from chephets, delight, pleasure, with the suffixes -i, my, and -bah, in her: my delight is in her.
biblical_def: The name appears twice, in two very different places. First as a mother: “Manasseh was twelve years old when he began to reign, and reigned fifty and five years in Jerusalem. And his mother's name was Hephzibah” (2 Kings 21:1). Hezekiah's queen bore a beautiful name and a son who filled Jerusalem with blood. Then as a promise: “Thou shalt no more be termed Forsaken; neither shall thy land any more be termed Desolate: but thou shalt be called Hephzibah, and thy land Beulah: for the LORD delighteth in thee, and thy land shall be married” (Isaiah 62:4). The forsaken city receives a bride's name, and the next verse explains it: “as the bridegroom rejoiceth over the bride, so shall thy God rejoice over thee” (Isaiah 62:5). The delight is not in Zion's merit but in the LORD's free choice of her, which is why the name can be given to a people that had been called Forsaken.

corruption_summary: God's delight in His people is turned into a general approval of everyone as they are, cut loose from the covenant and the Bridegroom who secures it.
corruption_paragraphs: Popular devotional writing lifts the LORD delighteth in thee out of Isaiah 62 and hands it to every reader as unconditional affirmation. The verse is a covenant promise to a redeemed Zion, given in the language of marriage, and it is fulfilled in the church as the bride of Christ.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition beyond that loosening. The principle to recover is that God's delight rests on His people in the Beloved. Hephzibah is a name given, not a quality discovered; the forsaken become the delight of God because the Bridegroom has betrothed them to Himself.

pos: proper n. (Hebrew prophetic name of the land of Israel)
etymology: Hebrew be'ulah, passive participle of ba'al, to marry, to be lord over: married, possessed as a wife.
biblical_def: Beulah occurs once, as the land's new name. “Thou shalt no more be termed Forsaken; neither shall thy land any more be termed Desolate: but thou shalt be called Hephzibah, and thy land Beulah: for the LORD delighteth in thee, and thy land shall be married” (Isaiah 62:4). The desolate land is pictured as a widow or an abandoned wife, and God declares her married. Isaiah had already given the ground of it: “For thy Maker is thine husband; the LORD of hosts is his name” (Isaiah 54:5). The marriage image runs from the prophets to the last pages of the Bible, where John sees the holy city “prepared as a bride adorned for her husband” (Revelation 21:2). Beulah is therefore not first a pleasant country but a covenant status: the land and people the LORD has taken to Himself, never again to be called Desolate.

corruption_paragraphs: The nineteenth-century gospel song Beulah Land, drawing on Bunyan's Country of Beulah in The Pilgrim's Progress, made the word a byword for the sweet borderland of heaven. Bunyan used it as allegory and knew what he was doing; later popular use often kept the sweetness and lost the marriage.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that Beulah means married. The comfort of the name rests entirely on the Husband: the LORD who made the land, redeemed the people, and will present the church to Himself as a bride without spot.

pos: proper n. (Hebrew name of the grandson of Eli)
etymology: Hebrew 'i-khabod, from 'i, where? or not, and kabod, glory, weight, honour: where is the glory? or no glory.
biblical_def: Ichabod was born on the worst day of Eli's house. The ark had been taken by the Philistines, Hophni and Phinehas were dead, and Eli had fallen and broken his neck. Phinehas' wife “was with child, near to be delivered: and when she heard the tidings that the ark of God was taken, and that her father in law and her husband were dead, she bowed herself and travailed” (1 Samuel 4:19). Dying, she named the boy for the catastrophe: “And she named the child Ichabod, saying, The glory is departed from Israel” (1 Samuel 4:21). Her last words gave the reason: “The glory is departed from Israel: for the ark of God is taken” (1 Samuel 4:22). The psalmist later saw the hand of God in it: He “delivered his strength into captivity, and his glory into the enemy's hand” (Psalm 78:61). Israel had treated the ark as a charm, and God let the charm be carried off.

corruption_summary: Ichabod is used as a pulpit taunt for any church in decline, when the text names something sharper: glory departing from a people who presumed upon the symbols of God's presence.
corruption_paragraphs: The name is easily turned into a slogan. The fall of Shiloh was not a matter of attendance or reputation. Israel carried the ark into battle as though the box could compel God, and the priests who handled it were men who despised His offerings. The glory departed because God withdrew it from a corrupt ministry and a superstitious people.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the outward signs of God's presence are no guarantee of it. Sacraments, buildings and heritage cannot hold God to a church that has abandoned His word, and only the true presence of God by His Spirit and word is a church's glory.

pos: proper n. (surname given by Christ to James and John)
etymology: Greek Boanerges, representing an Aramaic phrase, bene regesh or bene rogez; Mark himself interprets it: sons of thunder.
biblical_def: When the Lord ordained the twelve He renamed three of them: Simon became Peter, and of the sons of Zebedee Mark records: “And James the son of Zebedee, and John the brother of James; and he surnamed them Boanerges, which is, The sons of thunder” (Mark 3:17). Luke shows the thunder at work. A Samaritan village would not receive Jesus, “And when his disciples James and John saw this, they said, Lord, wilt thou that we command fire to come down from heaven, and consume them, even as Elias did?” (Luke 9:54). The answer was a rebuke: “Ye know not what manner of spirit ye are of” (Luke 9:55). The name did not flatter them; it described them, and grace went to work on what it described. James became the first apostle to die by the sword, and John, the son of thunder, became the apostle who wrote most of love.

corruption_summary: Boanerges is borrowed as a badge for a fiery temperament, as if Christ's surname were a commendation of zeal without knowledge.
corruption_paragraphs: Preachers and organizations have taken the name as a banner for boldness, and there is a genuine boldness that belongs to the gospel. But the only time the Gospels show the sons of thunder acting on their own fire, the Lord rebukes them. Zeal that would call down fire on the unreceptive is not the Spirit of Christ.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is sanctification: Christ names men as they are and makes them what He wills. The thunder of John was not removed but brought under the Spirit, so that his later letters thunder against error precisely because they burn with love for the truth.

pos: interj. (Aramaic word of command spoken by Christ)
etymology: Aramaic 'ethpattach or 'eppattach, passive imperative of petach, to open, transliterated into Greek as ephphatha; Mark interprets it: Be opened.
biblical_def: Mark preserves the very sound of the Lord's voice at the healing of a deaf man in Decapolis. Jesus took him aside, put His fingers into his ears, touched his tongue, “And looking up to heaven, he sighed, and saith unto him, Ephphatha, that is, Be opened” (Mark 7:34). The effect was immediate: “And straightway his ears were opened, and the string of his tongue was loosed, and he spake plain” (Mark 7:35). The word was a command, not a prayer, and the sigh was the sigh of the Son of God who felt the curse He was undoing. The miracle was a sign that the age of Isaiah's promise had come: “Then the eyes of the blind shall be opened, and the ears of the deaf shall be unstopped” (Isaiah 35:5). The ear Christ opens He opens by His word, and the gospel still comes to deaf sinners in no other way.

corruption_summary: Rome took Christ's word into its baptismal rite as a ceremony of touching ears and nostrils, adding to the ordinance what Christ never commanded.
corruption_paragraphs: The Roman baptismal rite, in its traditional form, includes an Effeta ceremony in which the priest touches the ears and nostrils of the candidate, historically with spittle, and pronounces the word. The ceremony borrows the gesture of a single miracle and makes it a fixed part of an ordinance. Christ did not command it, the apostles did not practice it, and the New Testament knows nothing of it.

The regulative principle of worship holds that what Scripture commands is required and what it has not commanded is not permitted. The church does not open ears by rite. Christ opens them sovereignly by His word and Spirit, and faith comes by hearing, and hearing by the word of God.

pos: n. (Aramaic word of the writing on the wall)
etymology: Aramaic teqel, from teqal, to weigh, cognate with the Hebrew shaqal and the shekel weight: weighed, or a shekel.
biblical_def: Belshazzar's feast ended with four words written by a hand on the plaster: “And this is the writing that was written, MENE, MENE, TEKEL, UPHARSIN” (Daniel 5:25). Daniel read them as a judicial sentence, and the third was aimed at the king himself: “TEKEL; Thou art weighed in the balances, and art found wanting” (Daniel 5:27). The pun lies in the word: a tekel is a shekel, a weight, and the king who drank from the temple vessels was put in God's scale and came up light. The sentence was carried out that night. David had long before said what the scales would show of any man weighed alone: “to be laid in the balance, they are altogether lighter than vanity” (Psalm 62:9). Every sinner is found wanting when weighed by himself, and only one Man was ever weighed and found full weight, and His righteousness is reckoned to all who believe.

corruption_summary: The writing on the wall is reduced to a proverb about bad omens, when Daniel read it as God's verdict on a king who defiled holy things.
corruption_paragraphs: To see the writing on the wall now means only to foresee trouble. Daniel's point was not prediction but judgment: God had numbered the kingdom, weighed the king, and divided the realm, because Belshazzar knew what had happened to his father and lifted himself up against the Lord of heaven anyway.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that God weighs men, and that no man passes the scale on his own merit. Tekel drives the sinner to the imputed righteousness of Christ.

biblical_def: Agur is known only by the chapter that bears his name. “The words of Agur the son of Jakeh, even the prophecy: the man spake unto Ithiel, even unto Ithiel and Ucal” (Proverbs 30:1). He begins by confessing his ignorance, and then asks the questions that silence human pride: “Who hath ascended up into heaven, or descended? who hath gathered the wind in his fists? who hath bound the waters in a garment? who hath established all the ends of the earth? what is his name, and what is his son's name, if thou canst tell?” (Proverbs 30:4). The question about the Son stands in the Old Testament as a door the New opens. Agur's answer to his own ignorance is not despair but revelation: “Every word of God is pure: he is a shield unto them that put their trust in him” (Proverbs 30:5). The man who knew himself brutish rested on a word he did not invent.

corruption_summary: Agur is recast as a skeptic, his confession of ignorance turned into agnosticism, when it is the doorway to faith in God's pure word.
corruption_paragraphs: Modern commentary often reads Proverbs 30:1-4 as the voice of a doubter who cannot know God, answered later by a pious editor. The chapter does not read that way. Agur confesses that he has not learned wisdom by his own climbing, and then he states the alternative: God has spoken, and every word of God is pure.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition beyond that skeptical reading. The principle to recover is humility before revelation. The man who knows he cannot ascend into heaven is the man ready to receive what has come down from it, and the Son whose name Agur asked is the One who descended.
